Overview/Deed amounts

Paper 01 · Deed amounts

When a Deed Is Not a Market Sale

Foreclosure Transfers, Statutory Consideration, and Repeat-Sales House-Price Measurement

Pablo LoschiEmpirical research

The short version

Some foreclosure deeds record a bid, judgment or discharged debt. Retaining flagged transfers changes the path of a retrospective New York house-price index. The size and even the direction can depend on classification, sale dates and which later resales enter the sample. In Philadelphia and New Jersey, lower recorded foreclosure amounts deepen the measured crash. The paper shows why a recorded amount needs a transaction screen, and why the screened index still carries uncertainty.

Read the paper PDFAnalysis archive

Paper version 1.0.12, 25 October 2026 · Sources and evidence update (ZIP). Baseline replication files remain linked from the archive.

The question

When a lender takes title through foreclosure or a deed in lieu, New York transfer-tax rules can base the recorded consideration on a bid, judgment or discharged debt rather than a negotiated price. Should that amount enter a house-price index as if it were a sale price?

The paper classifies such deeds by their parties in the 2003–2025 ACRIS extract for Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens, and measures what they do to a standard repeat-sales index.

Main findings

  • 16,655deeds flagged as legal-rule transfers among 1.47 million records, 2003–2025.
  • 62%of flagged transfers pass conventional sales screens.
  • +1.1log points: how far the unscreened index sits above the screened one on average in 2008–10 (95% interval 0.6 to 1.6).
  • −2.3log points: how far it sits below in 2011–12 (95% interval −2.8 to −1.7). The largest single-quarter gap is 3.7 log points, in 2010Q3.
  • 2.6log points in 2010Q3 when screening only the narrowest set of lender transfers (simultaneous 95% band across quarters: 0.9 to 4.4).

These comparisons hold the classifier’s labels fixed. The document-based uncertainty and alternative index specifications below can weaken or reverse the comparison.

Why it matters

About 94–95% of flagged transfers recorded in 2016–2025 appear in the city’s public sales file at their recorded amount.

  • Repeat-sales indices, hedonic models and local price series built from public deed records inherit these amounts unless deeds are classified by their parties: the document type does not distinguish them.
  • In the main fixed-label comparison, the raw index falls less into 2009–10 and more into 2011–12, which matters for short-window returns and borough comparisons. The hedonic comparison also changes around 2009–10. Its later path differs from the repeat-sales result, consistent with pairing contributing to the shortfall, without identifying that mechanism conclusively.
  • Dropping flagged pairs and bridging across them answer different questions; the choice moves the crisis decline by about five log points and should be made explicitly.
  • The classifier is released as a free, dependency-light Python module.
Index buildersUrban economistsUsers of ACRIS and DOF sales data

What the results can tell us

The fixed-label peak-to-trough contrast is −0.64 log points, with an interval from −3.03 to +1.25. It does not establish a different overall decline. The index comparison also depends on sale dating, the estimation horizon and how repeat-sale pairs are rebuilt.

The validation uses 40 human-reference readings. Weighted precision is 0.82 and foreclosure recall is 0.71, with wide finite-population intervals: 0.40–0.99 and 0.02–0.95, respectively. Historical agreement with AI readings does not establish accuracy, and these 40 readings do not validate the original 316 resolved AI classifications.

One model combining classification-rate uncertainty with parcel resampling gives a 2010Q3 difference of 2.25 log points, with a central 95% range of −0.21 to +4.53. That range depends on the model and the reference readings; it is not a design-based confidence interval. Some alternative specifications reverse the comparison. The screened index is therefore a sensitivity result, not a verified market-price correction.
